newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian Broadcasting Corp Midday Update.
newsitem.headline: Australian Broadcasting Corp Midday Update.

text.p: JABILUKA OPPONENTS UP THE STAKES
Conservation groups are turning up the heat on the Federal Government in an attempt to block approval for the Jabiluka uranium mine planned for the Northern Territory.
Opponents of the mine have threatened legal action and increased international pressure if the Federal Government approves the venture.
They say Jabiluka would impact on the World Heritage values of Kakadu National Park.
Dave Sweeney from the Australian Conservation Foundation says he expects the Environmental Impact Statement for Jabiluka tol be submitted to the Federal Government shortly.
Mr Sweeney says the Federal Government should show leadership, and reject the proposal.

But he says if this is not the case, the mine's opponents will explore every angle to try to stop it, including legal, community and targeted political action, and voicing concerns on the global stage.
HANSON'S PARTY TO SIGN THEM UP YOUNG
One Nation, the political party launched by Federal Independent M-P, Pauline Hanson, is to launch a youth branch called Youth Nation.
Miss Hanson's principal advisor, David Oldfield, says Youth Nation will cement the main party's future, and will be launched early in the new year, if not before.
Mr Oldfield says all political parties would be happy to have younger people involved, and in some other parties, membership is falling because members are dying off.
He says One Nation already has a diverse age range among its members.
Mr Oldfield says Young Nation will be the young version of One Nation.
KENNETT TO LOOK INTO BABY MEDICAL EXPERIMENTS
Victorian Premier, Jeff Kennett, says he is expecting more information about the use of babies in medical experiments this afternoon.
The Walter and Eliza Hall Institute of Medical Research says a herpes vaccine was tested on 16 children from the Broadmeadows Babies' Home, nearly 46 years ago.
Tests on orphaned and abandoned babies continued between 1945 and 1970.
Mr Kennett says his Government will look into the practice.
The Commonwealth Serum Laboratories says it cannot comment on protocols which took place when C-S-L was an arm of the Commonwealth Health Department, before 1961.
A pressure group for former wards of the state has expressed its outrage that the tests were allowed to go ahead, and has demanded an investigation to identify those used as human guinea pigs.
SKIING IN AUSTRALIA MAY BE A THING OF THE PAST IN THE FUTURE
Australia may have only one viable ski resort in 30 years if global warming forecasts are correct.

Research conducted by the A-N-U on temperature change shows that in the worst case scenario, average temperatures would rise by almost two degrees by the year 2030, and snowfall would drop by around 10 per cent.
That would leave Charlotte Pass as the only ski-resort with sufficient snowfalls to remain viable - the rest would have to rely on expensive snow-making.
Researchers say Australians may have to travel overseas to ski, and have suggested resort operators might have to look at alternative methods of attracting visitors.
However, they stress a great deal of uncertainty surrounds global warming, and it is hard to predict what will really happen.
BLACKHAWK CRASH COMPENSATION MAY RISE AFTER REVIEW

Federal Cabinet is today considering a recommendation to increase Defence Force compensation payments - a move which would lift the amount of money given to survivors of last year's Blackhawk tragedy and victims' families.
Defence Force Science and Personnel Minister, Bronwyn Bishop, ordered a review of the military compensation scheme after the tragedy.
She had been considering a review before that occurred because of concerns raised in the services about the scheme.
The maximum payout available under the current scheme is around $155,000.
Cabinet is expected to approve the recommendation which will backdate rises to April 1994, the starting date of the current scheme.
-- Reuters Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
